title: The Angels' Song - Luke 2:1-14
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
summary: Pastor Tito Lyro examines the magnificent choir of heavenly hosts singing praises at Jesus' birth, exploring what their song reveals about the nature, significance, and consequences of Christ's incarnation. The angels' simple but glorious proclamation—'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill toward men'—communicates that Jesus is God's final and complete revelation, brings reconciliation between God and humanity, and extends God's grace to believers.

outline.title: The Scene: God's Sovereign Preparation and the Humble Announcement
subpoints: God guides Caesar Augustus to decree a census that brings Mary and Joseph to Bethlehem, fulfilling Micah's prophecy
The shepherds—a despised and distrusted group—are chosen as the first recipients of the angels' announcement, proving the account is true history, not fabricated legend
One angel announces the birth; then suddenly the heavenly hosts join in praise

outline.title: The Nature of Christ's Birth: The Climax of Divine Revelation
subpoints: God has revealed himself throughout history through creation, the law, the sacrificial system, and the prophets
These previous revelations were veiled and incomplete—types and shadows of things to come
Jesus is God's final, full, and clear revelation of himself; in him dwells all the fullness of God bodily
The angels praise because the climax of all God's communication has arrived

outline.title: The Significance of Christ's Birth: Reconciliation and Peace with God
subpoints: Humanity was created for perfect union and peace with God, but sin destroyed that relationship
Jesus came to bring reconciliation between God and mankind—he is the only mediator
The peace the angels sing about is a God-wrought wholeness and completeness that passes all understanding
This peace is the satisfaction all hearts long for; without it, humanity searches endlessly for meaning and fulfillment

outline.title: The Consequence of Christ's Birth: God's Grace Extended to the Elect
subpoints: The grace of God is displayed and communicated to those who believe in Jesus
Those who refuse to believe actively reject the clear display of God's grace at the cross
Believers are saved by grace through faith, made God's workmanship, created for good works
This grace grants redemption from lawlessness and purifies a people zealous for good works

outline.title: The Response: Go, See, Worship, and Proclaim
subpoints: The shepherds' example teaches us how to respond: go to Jesus with haste
Unbelievers must trust in Christ for salvation without delay
Believers must run deeper into Christ, hold tighter to him, and delight more strongly in him
All must worship Jesus and make his worth widely known to others

transcript:
## The Reading of God's Word

> "And it came to pass in those days that a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered. This census first took place while Quirinius was governing Syria. So all went to be registered, every one to his own city. Joseph also went up from Galilee out of the city of Nazareth into Judea to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David. To be registered with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was with child. So it was that while they were there, the days were completed for her to be delivered. And she brought forth her firstborn son and wrapped him in swaddling cloths and laid him in a manger because there was no room for them in the inn. Now there were in the same country shepherds living out in the fields, keeping watch over their flock by night. And behold, an angel of the Lord stood before them and the glory of the Lord shone around them. And they were greatly afraid. Then the angel said to them, 'Do not be afraid, for behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which will be to all people. For there is born to you this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord. And this will be the sign to you: You will find a babe wrapped in swaddling cloths lying in a manger.' And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly hosts praising God and saying, 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill toward men.'" (Luke 2:1-14)

## The Majesty of the Angels' Song

Many of you know that I grew up in the Tacoma Bible church. For years, Tacoma Church had a Christmas cantata on the Sunday closest to Christmas. They would perform a great production—an hour long of singing. The choir would practice for weeks with serious practice on complicated songs, and they did a great job. But all the years that I attended the Christmas cantatas there in Tacoma, none of them were like the one we read here in Luke chapter two.

Sure, the Tacoma Church choir sang well. They sang elaborate songs, they sang many songs, but none of them compared to the glorious choir of angels that we read here in chapter two, verse 14. One simple song, one line, but what a glorious line that is when they say: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill toward men."

But as we think about that scene, have you ever stopped to think about it seriously? When you hear this text, is the first thing that comes to your mind the voice of the Peanuts characters singing on their show? Have you ever stopped to think about this seriously? Do you really consider what's going on here?

## Setting the Scene: God's Sovereign Guidance

Let's set the scene as we move toward verse 14. Do you ever notice what is going on here in verses 1 through 5? Here we have God guiding the heart of a wicked ruler, Caesar Augustus, to work and orchestrate everything so that Mary and Joseph end up in Bethlehem to register for that census that would only happen about every 14 years. This was so that Jesus would be born in that little town of Bethlehem, no more than a village, in order to fulfill the great prophecies concerning the Messiah of the Lord in Micah chapter 5.

While there in Bethlehem to register themselves in the census, Jesus arrives, and you're very familiar with that story there in verses 6 and 7. Following the birth of Jesus in that very meager condition in the stable—perhaps a cave where they kept animals—the most majestic Christmas cantata takes place in verses 8 through 14.

## The Significance of the Shepherds

Do you ever notice who the immediate audience of that cantata is? The immediate people that the angels are singing to—they're singing to the shepherds. That's an important fact because shepherds were one of the lowest and most despised groups of people in society. They were a group of people who really struggled with the truth. The shepherds of the first century had a reputation of being liars. They tended to struggle with the truth and they tended to struggle with other people's property.

This is not the group you would choose if you're trying to gain credibility for your story. If you're trying to make something up and you're trying to get credibility to a story that you're telling, you'd have the angel show up to the king or to the synagogue rulers or to the Pharisees. But they show up to the shepherds. And the only reason the shepherds are included here is because what Luke is telling us actually happened. There's no other reason to include a discredited group in your account unless you're not trying to gain credibility because what happened, what we read, actually happened.

It is to these shepherds that the angels come to announce the birth of the Savior of the world in verses 9 through 12. And as the angel finishes announcing the birth of the Savior, all heaven breaks forth in praising God in verse 13, much like the Hallelujah Chorus that we find in Revelation chapter 19 related to the second coming of our Savior, where the hosts of heaven sing: "Hallelujah, salvation and glory and honor and power belong to the Lord our God."

The content of their praise was glory to God and peace to mankind through the glorious Savior who was just born. That's what they're singing about.

## The Heavenly Hosts: God's Armies

As you read the story, if one angel wasn't enough, one angel shows up to the shepherds and the shepherds are afraid. That's a common theme in the Scriptures—when an angel shows up at your door, you are afraid. And he says, "Don't fear. Here is the glorious message of the gospel: a Savior has come to you."

And if that wasn't enough, then the hosts of heaven start to praise God for the birth of Jesus. In verse 13, Luke says: "Suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly hosts praising God."

Now, the heavenly hosts—we're used to using that word, and often we don't know what it means. The word "host" sometimes refers to when you're having people over your house and you're hosting them. But that's not how this word is used in the Bible. The idea of the hosts is the armies of God.

We have this idea of angels from Hallmark cards or little decorations or from Baroque paintings—these feminine perhaps, or chubby little guys with little tiny wings, looking at each other, blue-eyed and blonde. And yet the Bible says these are the very soldiers of God who go about doing his bidding, and they show up to sing about the birth of the Lord.

If you look at the examples in the Bible, we know the story of Elisha. In the Book of Second Kings, the Syrian army comes to town. As far as you can see are Syrian soldiers and chariots. Of course, they surround the town, and the prophet's servant is afraid and says, "We're doomed. Now we're done." But Elisha says, "I got this, just trust me." And then he prays that God would open the servant's eyes. When the servant's eyes are opened, he sees and says, "Behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha."

You've read about the angels in the Book of Revelation, especially Revelation 12. They're not these little cherubs that look like overweight children. They are the armies of heaven fighting for our very existence against the armies of Satan. And these are the ones singing about the birth of our Savior.

So we have this magnificent choir singing praises to God because his Son has been born.

## The Angels' Song: Three Essential Truths

The angels' song is simple. It's a simple song—one line, two clauses—that communicate three things to us. Look at verse 14: "Glory to God in the highest and on earth peace, goodwill toward men."

### Part One: The Nature of Christ's Birth—The Climax of Divine Revelation

The first thing it communicates is the nature of the birth of Jesus. The coming of Christ is the climax of divine self-revelation. The angels are praising God because God has given to the world the final, full, and clear revelation of himself.

God has revealed himself in many different ways. From the very beginning of time, God has made very clear who he is. Creation itself shouts his attributes. In Psalm 19 we read that "the heavens declare the glory of God and the firmament shows his handiwork." Paul gets even more precise than that. In Romans 1, verse 20, he says: "For since the creation of the world, his invisible attributes are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead, so that they are without excuse."

God has always been a God of revelation—a God who makes himself known. But humanity has refused to listen to what creation declares about its Creator. So God started speaking in a special way, directly or through messengers. He gave some people inspired visions that told them about what God was saying and thinking. He directed his people through his perfect law. He illustrated the need for atonement and forgiveness in the sacrificial system. He sent prophets to his people. These were great and gracious revelations from God, but they were veiled. They weren't as clear. They were types and shadows of the things to come.

So 2,000 years ago, God gloriously sent his Son to make all things clear. And that's why the author of Hebrews in Hebrews chapter 1 says:

> "God, who at various times and in various ways spoke in time past to the fathers by the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us by His Son, whom He has appointed heir of all things, through whom also He made the worlds, who being the brightness of His glory and the express image of His person, and upholding all things by the power of His word, when He had by Himself purged our sins, sat down at the right hand of the majesty on high, having become so much better than the angels as He has by inheritance obtained a more excellent name than they."

God revealed himself in his Son. In the Son, the fullness of God appears. And that's why we don't need any more revelation. How better can you get than Jesus? You can't perfect the perfect.

Paul says: "For in Him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily." (Colossians 2:9)

The armies of heaven are praising God and declaring that all glory belongs to him because the final revelation has come. He is the head of all rulers and he is the head of all authorities. John says:

> "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God, and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth." (John 1:1-3, 14)

This is the climax of all revelation. This is the climax of all communication from God. The point is that the angels of heaven can't contain themselves and break forth into singing.

So the first thing this song tells us is about the nature of the birth of Christ—the final revelation of God.

### Part Two: The Significance of Christ's Birth—Reconciliation and Peace

The second thing it communicates is the significance of the birth of Jesus. In order to understand this correctly, we need to talk about the wording of the second half of what the angels say.

Our translation says: "Glory to God in the highest and on earth peace, goodwill toward men."

The English Standard Version does a better job translating this last clause. It translates it this way: "And on earth peace among those with whom he is pleased."

Peace among those with whom he is pleased.

The birth of Jesus is significant to the world because it is through him that man and God are reconciled. That is the peace that the angels are singing about.

The Apostle Paul says: "Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." (Romans 5:1)

Christ Himself said in John 14:27:

> "Peace I leave with you, My peace I give to you; not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid."

Brothers and sisters, friends, visitors—humanity was created to be in perfect union and peace with God. But we sinned, and that unity, that peace, was destroyed. Jesus Christ came to bring that reconciliation between men and God.

Every single person in this room knows—whether you believe in Jesus Christ or not—that this is true. Everyone deep in our hearts knows that we are not at peace. You might say, "That's not the case, well why is it then that society, humanity in general is always searching for meaning, for fulfillment, for wholeness, for joy, for identity?" It's because they were created for those things. It's because of that union with God and their peace with God that being destroyed, our hearts are always yearning for that.

That is exactly what biblical peace is. Peace is a God-wrought wholeness, a God-wrought completeness. It is through this baby that the shepherds are about to meet that humanity and God can be brought back together.

Paul says: "For there is only one mediator, only one that can go between men and God, and that's the man Jesus Christ." (1 Timothy 2:5)

This peace that the angels are singing about—the believers share in this reconciliation. The Apostle Paul says in 2 Corinthians 5:

> "Now all things are of God, who has reconciled us to Himself through Jesus Christ, and has given us the ministry of reconciliation, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, not imputing their trespasses to them, and has committed to us the word of reconciliation. Now then, we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were pleading through us we implore you on Christ's behalf, be reconciled to God. For He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him."

This peace we all crave comes only through reconciliation with God because of the work of Christ. And it passes all understanding, as Paul tells us in Philippians 4. That's the only place you're going to find that peace.

So this song communicates to us the nature of Christ's birth. It communicates to us the significance of Christ's birth.

### Part Three: The Consequence of Christ's Birth—God's Grace to the Elect

The third thing it communicates is the consequence of the birth of Jesus. The angels are saying that peace comes to those with whom he is pleased—those are the objects of God's grace. The grace of God is displayed to those who believe in Him through Jesus. The abundant grace of God is communicated to His elect.

In Titus, the apostle says:

> "For the grace of God that brings salvation has appeared to all men, teaching us that denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly in the present age, looking for the blessed hope and the glorious appearing of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for us, that He might redeem us from every lawless deed and purify for Himself His own special people, zealous for good works."

Now here's what I want you to hear: "The grace of God that brings salvation has appeared to all men." Because every one of you that don't believe in Jesus Christ is willingly refusing to see the grace of God revealed to you.

I don't know if you've ever read "The Last Battle." It's the last book in the sequence of the fictional Narnia story. It's not necessarily the last book written, but it's the last one in the series. In one of the last scenes, there are people sitting around a fire and they're refusing to look around and see that they're in heaven, that they're around them. They feel they're interested in the grace of God displayed, and those that don't believe in Jesus are doing that. They're actively refusing to see what God has clearly displayed in the cross of Jesus Christ.

The grace of God that brings salvation has appeared to all men, teaching us that denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly in the present age, looking for the blessed hope and the glorious appearing of the great God and Savior Jesus Christ, who gave Himself for us that He might redeem us from every lawless deed and purify for Himself His own special people, zealous for good works.

That's us who believe.

Do you believe that Jesus Christ came into the world in order to reconcile you to God and to grant you that fullness that you so long for? If you do, then these words that I'm going to read next are true of you:

> "For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, but a gift of God, so that no one can boast. And in that salvation God created you. He made you a new creation. His workmanship, created for good works, created to praise Him, to obey Him, to glorify Him, that you should walk in them."

That's Ephesians 2:8-10.

## How Should We Respond?

So what should we do with this information? What do we do with it? Because the Bible doesn't want you just to listen to things and say, "Deep, deep" or "Good sermon" at the end. The Bible calls you to listen and to act. Either be really angry about what I'm saying or do something with the things that the Bible says. Don't park in neutral. What happens if you park a car in neutral on a hill? It rolls, and that's the end of it most of the time.

So how do we do this? What do you do? What do we do with this information? How do we respond to the truth that the armies of heaven are praising God because Jesus came to reconcile man to God and to grant them wholeness?

Well, the shepherds teach us what to do. Look at verse 15:

> "So it was, when the angels had gone away from them into heaven, that the shepherds said to one another, 'Let us now go to Bethlehem and see this thing that has come to pass, which the Lord has made known to us.'"

What do we do? We go see Jesus. That's what the shepherds did. We go see Jesus. We run to him. We don't delay.

If you have never done that, do it now. Trust in him for salvation for your souls. You're not guaranteed the next breath, so do it now.

But if you are already trusting in Christ, don't stop. Keep on going to him for the constant peace that comes from him. If you are in Christ, run deeper into him. Cling tighter to him. Delight more strongly in him.

And then worship him.

The shepherds in verse 16—Luke tells us:

> "They came with haste and found Mary and Joseph and the babe lying in a manger."

They went and worshiped Jesus.

And then they could not contain themselves. What did they do next? In verse 17:

> "They made it widely known the same day what they had seen."

Then we tell others about Jesus.

So do something with what you're hearing today. Believer or unbeliever, do something with what you're hearing here today.

Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among those with whom He is pleased. That is the angels' song. Christ Jesus came to reconcile men to God.
